overviewHtml:
This ungraded knowledge check assesses your understanding of Brentano's thesis of intentionality and how his students reworked it. You'll be asked about intentional inexistence, Brentano's classes of mental acts, the mark-of-the-mental thesis, Twardowski's distinction between content and object, and the problem of objects that don't exist.

Note: Use this to test yourself, review the feedback on any questions you miss, and retry until you feel confident before moving forward.

forms.stemHtml: In Brentano's phrase "intentional inexistence," what does "inexistence" mean?

options.html: The nonexistence of the object outside the mind
options.text: The nonexistence of the object outside the mind
options.feedbackHtml: Sorry, that's incorrect. The prefix in- means "in," not "not." Inexistence is the object's existence in the mental act as its object, whether or not it exists outside the act.

options.html: The existence of the object in the mental act as its object
options.text: The existence of the object in the mental act as its object
options.feedbackHtml: Correct! "Inexistence" means existence in. For Brentano, every mental act contains an object in this sense, whether or not the object exists outside the act.

options.html: The existence of the object only in the physical world
options.text: The existence of the object only in the physical world
options.feedbackHtml: Sorry, that's incorrect. Brentano's phrase concerns how an object exists in a mental act, not in the physical world. Inexistence is the object's existence in the mental act as its object.

options.html: The existence of the mental act without any body
options.text: The existence of the mental act without any body
options.feedbackHtml: Sorry, that's incorrect. The phrase concerns the object of a mental act, not the act's relation to a body. Inexistence is the object's existence in the mental act as its object.

forms.stemHtml: Which experience is most often cited as a challenge to Brentano's claim that every mental phenomenon is directed at an object?

options.html: A judgment that it will rain heavily tomorrow
options.text: A judgment that it will rain heavily tomorrow
options.feedbackHtml: Sorry, that's incorrect. A judgment affirms or denies an object, here rain tomorrow, so it fits Brentano's thesis. The standard challenges are moods and bodily sensations, such as a diffuse anxiety that isn't about anything in particular.

options.html: A sudden desire for a strong cup of coffee
options.text: A sudden desire for a strong cup of coffee
options.feedbackHtml: Sorry, that's incorrect. A desire is directed at what is desired, here coffee, so it fits Brentano's thesis. The standard challenges are moods and bodily sensations, such as a diffuse anxiety that isn't about anything in particular.

options.html: A diffuse anxiety about nothing in particular
options.text: A diffuse anxiety about nothing in particular
options.feedbackHtml: Correct! Moods like diffuse anxiety don't seem to be directed at any object, so they challenge the claim that all mental phenomena are intentional. Defenders of the thesis reply that such moods may be directed at the world as a whole.

options.html: A memory of a conversation from yesterday
options.text: A memory of a conversation from yesterday
options.feedbackHtml: Sorry, that's incorrect. A memory is directed at what is remembered, here the conversation, so it fits Brentano's thesis. The standard challenges are moods and bodily sensations, such as a diffuse anxiety that isn't about anything in particular.

forms.stemHtml: Which of the following are Brentano's three basic classes of mental acts? (Select all that apply.)

options.html: Presentations
options.text: Presentations
options.feedbackHtml: Correct! Presentation, having something before the mind, is the basic class. Every other act either is a presentation or is based on one.

options.html: Judgments
options.text: Judgments
options.feedbackHtml: Correct! Judgments accept or reject a presented object as existing.

options.html: Physical phenomena
options.text: Physical phenomena
options.feedbackHtml: Sorry, that's incorrect. For Brentano, physical phenomena are the contents that sensation presents, such as colors and sounds, not a class of mental acts.

options.html: Phenomena of love and hate
options.text: Phenomena of love and hate
options.feedbackHtml: Correct! This class takes a positive or negative stance toward a presented object, and includes emotion, desire, and will.

options.html: Inner observations
options.text: Inner observations
options.feedbackHtml: Sorry, that's incorrect. Inner observation isn't one of Brentano's three classes. The three classes are presentations, judgments, and phenomena of love and hate.

forms.stemHtml: How does Twardowski distinguish the content of a presentation from its object?

options.html: The content is the physical thing, and the object is the mental image of it
options.text: The content is the physical thing, and the object is the mental image of it
options.feedbackHtml: Sorry, that's incorrect. Twardowski places the content in the mind, not in the physical world. The content exists in the mind with the act, while the object is what is presented and may not exist.

options.html: The content exists in the mind with the act, and the object may not exist
options.text: The content exists in the mind with the act, and the object may not exist
options.feedbackHtml: Correct! For Twardowski, the content is the mental item through which the act is directed. The object is what the presentation is of, and it may not exist. The object also has properties the content lacks.

options.html: The content is what is judged, and the object is what is felt
options.text: The content is what is judged, and the object is what is felt
options.feedbackHtml: Sorry, that's incorrect. Twardowski's distinction applies within every presentation, not between judging and feeling. The content exists in the mind with the act, while the object is what is presented and may not exist.

options.html: The content and the object are two names for one mental entity
options.text: The content and the object are two names for one mental entity
options.feedbackHtml: Sorry, that's incorrect. Twardowski's point is that they're distinct. The content exists in the mind with the act, while the object is what is presented and may not exist.

forms.stemHtml: Meinong held that an object's is independent of its , so a golden mountain can be golden without existing.

options.html: being-so
options.text: being-so
options.feedbackHtml: Correct! For Meinong, what an object is like, its being-so (Sosein), doesn't depend on whether it exists.

options.html: content
options.text: content
options.feedbackHtml: Sorry, that's incorrect. Content is Twardowski's term for the mental item in a presentation. Meinong's principle concerns an object's being-so, what it is like.

options.html: act
options.text: act
options.feedbackHtml: Sorry, that's incorrect. The act is the mental occurrence, not a feature of the object. Meinong's principle concerns an object's being-so, what it is like.

options.html: content
options.text: content
options.feedbackHtml: Sorry, that's incorrect. Meinong's principle separates what an object is like from its being, whether it exists.

options.html: being
options.text: being
options.feedbackHtml: Correct! Meinong's principle is the independence of being-so (Sosein) from being (Sein).

options.html: presentation
options.text: presentation
options.feedbackHtml: Sorry, that's incorrect. A presentation is a kind of mental act. Meinong's principle separates what an object is like from its being, whether it exists.

title: Brentano's Intentionality
